newsitem.title: UK: UK protest against far-right election broadcast.
newsitem.headline: UK protest against far-right election broadcast.

text.p: More than 100 people demonstrated in the rain outside BBC headquarters in London on Friday, waving banners and chanting in protest at the broadcast of an election message by an extreme-right political party.
Police ushered the protesters behind barriers and stood guard, wary because previous anti-racism demonstrations have erupted into clashes with supporters of the British National Party (BNP).
But there was no sign of any rival protest before the five-minute campaign film for Britain's May 1 general election was aired by the BBC on Friday evening.
The National Assembly against Racism said it was holding demonstrations across Britain at the offices of broadcasters who planned to show the film later on Friday.

One independent company, Channel Four, refused to broadcast the message by the BNP, which wants to repatriate non-whites and has been blamed by anti-racist groups for a number of racially motivated attacks.

At Channel Four's request, the BNP had submitted a slightly cut version of the film, removing scenes of London streets populated with black people and a school with signs written in Urdu. But the broadcaster said this still failed to meet its standards code.
The BBC left those scenes in the film, but took out another in which a mother and her children were clearly identifiable.

The BBC says it was obliged to air the BNP's broadcast under election rules which grant free air time to any party fielding more than 50 candidates in the May 1 election. The BNP is standing 56 candidates.

The film opened with the BNP's leader John Tyndall standing beside the famous white cliffs of Dover on Britain's south coast and denouncing British leaders for handing over power to Europe and allowing foreign imports to destroy British industry.
It went on to show the scenes of parts of London where there are large black and Asian populations as Tyndall asked: "Do you want the rest of Britain to end up like this?"
The BNP has never won a seat in parliament. Its best result was in May 1994, when Tyndall won 1,511 votes, 7.03 percent of the vote, in the London seat of Dagenham.
The anti-racism demonstrators objected that the BNP's broadcast was being financed by Britons of all races who pay the annual licence fee that funds the BBC.
Tyndall said the demonstrators "had a nerve".
"Why the hell shouldn't we have a broadcast? It's supposed to be a democracy, a free society, and I find their views as objectionable as they find ours," he told Reuters.
"These people are really relics from Stalin's Russia."
The BNP's election message was the second this week to run into difficulties.

The Pro-Life Alliance, an anti-abortion party, on Thursday lost its High Court bid to try to stop television companies from cutting parts of its film. The judge ruled that scenes showing "mangled and mutilated" foetuses were too shocking for broadcast.
